title: Effects of physical exercise, LEGO, and Minecraft activities on anxiety in children with autism
author: Lo, Lowery, et al.

steps.title: LEGO: Introduce and set rules
steps.instruction: For the first five minutes, introduce the child to the student researcher and together create the LEGO session rules.

steps.title: LEGO: Engineer role (15 min)
steps.instruction: Assign the child the “engineer” role and the researcher the “builder” role; the engineer verbally describes needed pieces and assembly directions while the builder collects pieces and assembles the model for approximately 15 minutes.

steps.title: LEGO: Builder role (15 min)
steps.instruction: Switch roles so the child becomes the “builder” and the researcher the “engineer”; the child follows directions, gathers pieces, and builds the model for another 15 minutes.

steps.title: LEGO: Cleanup and debrief
steps.instruction: During the final 15 minutes, clean up all LEGO bricks and ask the child the reflection questions: Was it hard or easy? What are your strengths and weaknesses? What do you want to work on?

steps.title: Minecraft: Introduce and set goal
steps.instruction: For the first five minutes, introduce the child to the student researcher, set up two computers and headsets, and discuss the session goal (e.g., make basic wood tools, craft a bed, build an animal farm toward a two‑story shelter).

steps.title: Minecraft: Daytime task (20 min)
steps.instruction: Assign the agreed‑upon goal to the child; together, using verbal communication via headsets, work in daytime mode to achieve the goal for approximately 20 minutes.

steps.title: Minecraft: Night mode survival (20 min)
steps.instruction: Switch the game to night mode; for the first 15 minutes, cooperate to survive the night using the items created, then spend the remaining 5 minutes discussing how the session felt (Was it hard or easy? What are your strengths and weaknesses? What do you want to work on for the next session?).

description: The results of this study are described in “The Effects of a Physical Exercise Program, LEGO and Minecraft Activities on Anxiety in Underserved Children with Autism Spectrum Disorder” [25]. Anxiety scores, as measured by the parent-rated CBCL DSM-5 anxiety subscale and the self-rated SCARED, showed improvements at weeks 3, 6, and 8 in both physical exercise and sedentary play groups, with no significant differences between groups. CSHQ-ATN sleep scores improved in the physical exercise group during weeks 6 and 8, but not in the sedentary play group with no significant difference between LEGO activity and Minecraft activity subgroups. Salivary cortisol did not show any significant changes from baseline to post-intervention in either group. The PAQ-C scores showed that physical activity level was increased in the physical exercise group compared to the sedentary play group at week 8.
